Ridden: 2026 Aprilia RS 660 Made Me Feel Younger for a Day
56 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I live near a city where motorcycles are quite popular, with more and more of them showing up on public roads each year. It’s quite a big hub for the phenomenon, with one event bringing in thousands of riders to celebrate their love for bikes of all shapes and sizes.
I’ve noticed an interesting phenomenon: every high school in town has at least five or six motorcycles parked outside. It’s usually a line-up of Yamaha R125s and Honda CBR125s, but these days CFMoto models have become a popular option due to their affordability.
I’m going to sound old here for a moment, but “back in my day” there was only one highly-desirable option out there: the Aprilia RS 125. I’m obviously talking from the perspective of someone who only cared about riding bikes on public roads and not through forests. I think I must have been roughly 12 when I realized how much I wanted an RS 125.
Back then, it was an aspirational machine, as the RS 50 and Yamaha TZR50 were slightly more accessible, and some people thought they could avoid getting a motorcycle license by choosing this option. Spoiler alert: they couldn’t. Anyway, I haven’t seen an RS 125 on public roads in ages, and it pains me to say that.
In trying to deal with the downsides of a 2-stroke engine, the switch to a 4-stroke setup may have robbed it of its magic. But the world has changed over the past 20 years, and companies that want to survive in the new environment have no choice but to adapt.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution I’ve seen what my nephew is like: he thinks my RX-7 is cool but can’t stand dealing with the smell of oil and gasoline, the noise and the driving particularities of it all. I’m not even saying he’s wrong, as I realize I might just be too nostalgic to observe the progress. But I have to say that even after I’ve ridden dozens of fast motorcycles over the past eight years, I still want an RS 125 in my garage.
And that should explain why I’ve been curious about Aprilia’s RS660 from the moment I saw it at the 2019 EICMA show. By that point in my life, I had realized the RS125 just wouldn’t satisfy my “need for speed”. And all I could think about was spending a few years in the saddle of my Suzuki SV650S before moving on to either an Aprilia RSV Mille or an RSV4. Being a novice rider, all I could think about was that sort of progression.
But I’ve since learned having a liter bike on the road might just be too much, especially if you plan on sticking to the speed limit. You live and you learn, you grow old and you (technically) grow wiser. And while part of me is still screaming “get an early 2000s 600cc machine”, the “wise” part realizes that’s still too extreme for road-use/commuting. So maybe all these new middle-weight sport bikes we can opt for now are on on to something.
I decided I’ve waited too long for a shot at riding the RS660 , and phoned up the people at The Bike Hub in Bucharest, Romania to ask if I could borrow one for the day. They were happy to help out, and I’ve walked in enough motorcycle dealerships to know these guys are truly passionate about bikes. To me, that’s a crucial factor in deciding where to buy my next ride from.
Design Evaluation Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution People will often tell you that if you don’t look back at your car after you’ve parked it, you’ve bought the wrong car. I still get “I can’t believe I’m driving this after so many years of wanting one” every single time I’m in my RX-8, and it’s even more intense when I switch into the FC.
There are only a few things I miss about living in the big city: being able to order pizza or Chinese food, going karting with my friends, and what some would call “speedhunting”. I often enjoy walking through a neighborhood just to see what bikes or cool cars I can spot.
And I’ll stop, stare and take photos of one as often as I can. What I’m trying to say here is that the RS660 is the kind of machine that will have that same effect on me.
I could almost feel my knees shaking when I first saw it in the showroom, but I couldn’t fully appreciate it until it was out front and not surrounded by all the other bikes and scooters inside.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution To me, the only other machine in this class that comes close to looking as exciting is the Yamaha R7. It really does feel like a baby RSV4, and I’m sure you’ll agree my Alpinestars leathers and Ruroc AT4.0 Cobra Track helmet (which I’ve become fond of) are a much better match for the Aprilia than they were for the BMW F900 GSA .
I’m somewhat disappointed you can’t order a new RS660 in Acid Yellow anymore, but the new Venom Yellow/black finish (with the red wheels) is growing on me as it feels more in tone with Aprilia’s legacy.
You can still opt for Blue Marlin or the slightly more extreme Shakedown Yellow if you don’t mind spending a bit more for the Factory version of the bike. The front winglets will make you feel like a MotoGP rider for the day (which is great considering now has three riders in the Top 4 rankings, with Jorge Martin leading the way on his RS-GP26).
Every single angle of the RS660 is exactly what you’d dream of for a motorcycle in its class, and I must’ve looked at the photos my colleague took over 100 times now. The only element I can’t fully wrap my head around is how short the tail is, and I can just hear my wife blatantly refusing to ride pillion.
Riding Take Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution I want to make it clear from the get-go that this is by no means a definitive review of the RS660, as there’s only so much ground you can cover in five or six hours riding through a busy city. And it’s obvious I could only explore half of the RS660’s story, as it deserves a few laps at the racetrack (or at least some twisties) to show its true potential. I will tell you this: it made me feel younger for a day.
It put a huge smile on my face that I couldn’t shake for days, and I know it had to be just an appetizer for the time being. If I were to decide on buying a brand-new motorcycle, it would definitely be on the short list.
Also, I might ask for a longer session next so we can come up with a more detailed video and story on what it’s like. I doubt it will happen this year, as temperatures in my area have already plummeted, but I’ll think about it for 2027.
I picked the bike up in a busy part of town, and I guess my knees weren’t just shaking because of how pretty it looked like. I had ridden the Honda CBR650R at the racetrack back in 2023, and let’s just say I hadn’t thought about it since.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution The moment I swung my leg over the RS660 was heartwarming to say the least. It had taken me 20 years to finally ride an Aprilia sports bike, and I knew it would be considerably more thrilling than the old RS125 I used to dream about during my teenage years.
I was slightly concerned that the 659 cc parallel-twin engine would be disappointing, as I’m still stuck thinking a V-configuration would have been the better choice. Let’s not forget that the RS660’s engine is derived from its big bro’s V4, and with the 270 degree crankshaft design you could fool anyone into thinking it’s a V2 setup. Seeing is believing, and what happened next is the reason why I advise anyone to go out for a test ride before making a purchase.
All my concerns were blown away the moment I had a clear path in front of me. I rode away in “Commute”, and didn’t even switch to the Dynamic for the first 30 minutes. Once you hit 4,000 rpm you start to understand why the RS660 is such a popular choice these days, even though peak torque (52 lb-ft/71 NM) comes in at 8,400 rpm. You’ll have to go even higher than that for peak power (105 hp), and I guess that’s one excuse to rev it up to 10,400 rpm.
I realize different people will have a different experience riding any motorcycle, but I can say giving it the full twist of the wrist wasn’t terrifying (which is probably one of the ways you can define this category of bikes).
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution It also didn’t feel underwhelming like it did on the CBR650R. The throttle response is slightly better in Dynamic, and I almost couldn’t shake the feeling that the whole bike felt more eager to break the speed limit.
And while the Traction Control, Wheelie Control and Engine Braking characteristics change when using this riding mode, there’s no intervention for the Kayaba suspension front or rear. On the road, I didn’t even feel the need for an adjustment like that, and I imagine going for the Factory version of the motorcycle is the way to go if you intend to spend most of the time at the track.
That’s because it comes standard with Ohlins parts front and rear, which should explain the $2,300 price difference (according to data available for the US market). To me, the RS660 felt extremely compliant, flickable and nimble all at once, and its wet weight of only 183 kg is just one part of the equation. Both variations of the model use the same double 320 mm floating disc with Brembo radial calipers up front, and a 220 mm disc with Brembo calipers in the rear.
Modulating the latter while squeezing through traffic at low speeds felt like second nature, with the front brake always rising to the occasion every time I required it to. Again, it was all a sensible test, and the RS660 aced every road-going challenge. It was enough for me to recommend it to my buddy Omar, who is currently looking for a new motorcycle as he’s had enough dealing with the gremlins on a 25+ year old bike ( my old SV650S ).
Everyday Living Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution When I picked up the RS660, it had roughly half a tank of gas left in it with an estimated range of almost 100 miles (161 km). The tank’s capacity is 4 gallons (15 liters) and chances are you could ride it for almost 200 miles (321 km) if you behave.
You probably won’t be able to play nice, though, as it’s just too fun to keep going through the gear, especially since it has an up/down quickshifter as standard.
I’m not quite used to a modern setup like this having ridden mostly older bikes, and I found myself using the clutch on multiple occasions at least in the first part of the day.
I’m also not experienced enough to do away with all the rider aids, which is strange considering my previous phrase. I didn’t have any rider aids before and I was fine that way, but there’s some peace of mind that comes “packaged” with that sort of tech.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution The RS660 makes for a spirited commute, with an accent on spirited. There’s still some comfort to enjoy there, and the proof for that lies in the fact that I didn’t have to deal with any wrist or lower back pain after several hours of riding.
But you can see that it wants to go fast, and I’d say it’s a shame if you bought one and never tracked it. The “base” RS660 starts at $11,849 in the US, while the Factory version takes it up a notch to $14,149. I’m not saying the standard exhaust isn’t enough, but I also think a bike like this needs the SC Project system to really score a 5 out of 5.
I would also go for the TPMS and maybe even the carbon belly pan, and those two alone could add about $1,000 in extra cost. So yes, the RS660 is more expensive than the CBR650R, the Daytona 660, the R7 and the GSX8R.
I haven’t ridden the latter three, but after hours of watching and reading countless reviews online, I’m sure my money would go to Italy. I’ll make it a priority to test them all in 2027 for a more accurate conclusion.
Conclusion Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution Speaking of which, the only reason I’m not rating this bike a 5 out of 5 isn’t because it didn’t have the SC Project exhaust. It’s because I didn’t get to ride it away from traffic, on the track or one of my local mountain roads.
I have no doubt I’d be the limiting factor there, but I’m aiming to become a better rider with each passing year. I’ve looked at every single motorcycle manufacturer on the market, and I can honestly say that I would immediately opt for the Aprilia RS660 if part of me didn’t still think about exploring the continent on an F900 GSA.
That’s an internal battle I have to deal with, although I realize the only satisfying decision would be to get them both. That said, I think the RS660 works great if you’re still in your early years of riding (ideally if you’ve already racked up some miles on something with less power) but also when you’ve already been in the saddle for a while.
It has been my desktop wallpaper for several days now, and I know we must meet again sometime soon.
Rating: 4.5/5 Pros Exciting, MotoGP inspired looks that make every other bike in this category look boring or silly by comparison (except for the Yamaha R7). I’ll list this in the “Cons” section too, just because I needed to fill in the blanks, but the engine and exhaust combo are thrilling to listen to and use even in stock form It strikes the right balance between sportiness and comfort, without being too harsh on your wrists and lower back or shying away its racing DNA.
Cons not really the bike’s fault, but it does feel a bit crammed if you’re 6 feet tall (183 cm) and weigh over 210 pounds (95kg). nostalgia speaking here again but I wish we could go back to a mix of an analog tachometer and a smaller, complementary digital dash my third concern has to do with the standard exhaust system. It’s too tame for my taste, but there’s an easy fix as Aprilia offers an optional, road-legal, SC Project exhaust system for roughly 2,184 Euro/ $2,443 (Romanian market price)
